We will see whether or not an EWRC is occurring with #Dorian when recon arrives in a few hours - even if a ring forms on radar, it has to be accompanied by an outer wind maximum to be capable of disrupting the inner eyewall and triggering an EWRC.

@AnthonyFarnell @RyanMaue It is a bit early to say for sure that an EWRC is beginning with #Dorian - storms at this intensity can have "false starts" where the inner eyewall is just too intense to disrupt. Irma showed this pattern several times and took two days to eventually undergo an EWRC.

One potential problem with #Dorian is if it does complete an EWRC before turning north - besides making more of the Bahamas see hurricane conditions, it might be able to fully re-strengthen as it couples with the mid-latitude jet before it gets far enough north to be sheared.

This would produce a large, resilient and intense core over the Gulf Stream, which could mean #Dorian weaken more slowly as it approaches NC/SC due to the shear and be more likely to bring eyewall conditions onshore even if the center passes 20-30 miles east of the coast.

Day after day, for better than a week, the intensity of Hurricane Dorian has exceeded the predictions of the best available models -- exceeded them to a degree that makes the models seem ludicrous. They're not. But it takes a closer look to see why.

This is NOT an attack on the model. The models used by both the National Hurricane Center and European agencies have been refined to the point where they may be, quite literally, very close to as good as they can get.

For what we consider a “normal” storm the models do a genuinely fantastic job of defining how a storm will behave hours and days in advance. But there's more going on here than just "Dorian isn't a normal storm."

Because there's another model to consider. Or actually, a whole group of them. And those models are telling us that our models of hurricane behavior are already becoming LESS accurate, and may continue to miss the mark.

Models that look at how the world is being impacted by the climate crisis predict that we won’t necessarily have more hurricanes as the world warms, but we will have slower-moving, higher-moisture storms. Which are exactly those storms, like Dorian, where the models fall short.

Regarding Dorian, the theory suggests a minimum central pressure over the Bahamas on the order of 890mb is possible.  The central pressure of 913mb (11AM 9/1), while low, is above the potential minimum central pressure.  A similar comment can be made on wind speed as well.
